extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and readers of American government / political science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the textbook's enumerated categories of territorial governance and the fundamental constitutional limitations on state power (taxing, commerce, monetary, criminal, contracts), with supporting examples and cases. Intended to guide understanding of how federal law constrains state and territorial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: First group of territories (organized with local government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Territories that are "organized" with established local governments — example: Hawaii (annexed Aug. 12, 1898). Governor and secretary appointed by the President and Senate; legislature consists of a senate and a house of representatives elected by popular vote. Voter qualifications (example given): male U.S. citizen, twenty-one years of age, resident in the territory at least one year, duly registered, able to read, write, and speak either English or the local language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes note that each territory has a delegate in Congress who may speak but not vote. Footnote references (Willoughby) and literacy/registration requirements noted; example shows how federal appointments and local elections combine in organized territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Porto Rico governance under the organic act (second-group territory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the organic act (May 1, 1900) Porto Rico's inhabitants were not conferred U.S. citizenship but were "deemed citizens of Porto Rico"; they owe permanent allegiance to the U.S. but are not American citizens. The governor is appointed by the President and Senate for four years; six executive officers (secretary, attorney-general, treasurer, auditor, commissioner of the interior, commissioner of education) appointed similarly and performing both administrative functions and serving as members of the upper house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislature bicameral: upper house (executive council) comprised of the six executive officials plus five other persons 'of good repute' appointed by President and Senate, with at least five native inhabitants required; lower house of thirty-five members elected biennially under a franchise giving practically every adult male (meeting residence requirements) the right to vote. Notes friction from appointive vs representative branches and example of 1908-09 budget deadlock and Congressional remedy (continuation of prior year's financial arrangements). Footnotes discuss exclusions via literacy requirements and demographic shifts affecting political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippine governance under U.S. authority (second-group territory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development in three stages: (1) initial military government while many inhabitants were in revolt; (2) civil commission (Taft) to establish civil government and transfer of civil powers to that commission; (3) 1902 organic act providing for a legislative assembly after census and pacification, with the first representative assembly opening Oct. 16, 1907. Executive government vested in a commission of nine (including the governor) — five Americans and four Filipinos — appointed by the President and Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislature consists of the Philippine commission acting as upper house and an elected assembly for areas not inhabited by Moros/non-Christian tribes. Franchise limited by qualifications: oath of allegiance and requirement that voter be a property-owner, taxpayer, or able to read, write, and speak English or Spanish. The treatment emphasizes geographic, ethnic, and linguistic complexity (3,141 islands; ~30 tribes) and congressional difficulty in devising suitable government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third group of territories (direct federal governance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Territories governed directly by federal officers without any legislative assembly (examples: Guam, Tutuila/Samoa, Panama Canal Zone). These are administered by naval officers or executive appointees acting with full executive and legislative authority for the post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Samoa governed by a naval officer at Pago Pago; Guam governed by a naval officer; Panama Canal Zone initially governed by an isthmian canal commission under the President, later by a governor appointed for four years by the President and Senate with other officials holding office at the President's pleasure. Congressional law allowed exemptions (e.g., coastwise trade toll exemptions), and examples note international protests (Great Britain) and Congressional refusal to yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: District of Columbia governance (federal municipal control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress assumes the legislative powers of the District; executive power vested in a board of three commissioners (two civilians and one military) appointed by the President and Senate. The commissioners exercise large administrative powers and make ordinances relating to public safety, health, and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical experiments with mayor-and-council failed; in 1874 Congress abolished popular representation and the entire population became disfranchised (at the time). Congress sets aside specific days to handle District business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cuba under U.S. protection and the Piatt Amendment conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not a dependency, Cuba was placed under U.S. protection in 1898 for pacification. The joint resolution disclaimed intent to exercise sovereignty except for pacification, and promised to leave government to the people. The 1901 Piatt Amendment, incorporated into the army appropriation act, required that the Cuban constitution recognize U.S. protection and the right of American intervention under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: armed uprising in 1906 led to U.S. intervention and occupation until Jan. 1909 when elected native government was restored. Readings cited for background/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: States cannot lay and collect imposts and duties on exports and imports
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental constitutional limitation: states may not lay taxes on imports and exports except to defray expenses of inspection laws and only with the consent of Congress. A duty upon imports is a duty on the thing imported (Brown v. Maryland); while an import remains in original package/warehouse it is protected from state taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that foreign commerce is protected from state-imposed impediments. Footnote citations and discussion of when imported goods lose their 'import' character (incorporated/mixed into mass of property) and become taxable by the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: States cannot lay tonnage duties without consent of Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: States are forbidden to impose tonnage duties (a duty measured by a ship's internal capacity) without Congressional consent. While states may tax ships as property, taxes upon ships as instruments of commerce/navigation fall under the constitutional prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the Supreme Court's holding that the prohibition is general and applies regardless of ship ownership; cites State Tonnage Tax Cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: States cannot tax federal instrumentalities in ways that impair federal functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived from federal system logic: the power to create implies preservation; state taxation of federal instrumentalities or franchises that would 'retard, impede, burden, or in any manner control' federal laws or operations is impermissible. Modern modification: states may tax federal property so long as the tax does not impair the efficiency of the federal function — e.g., may tax buildings of a national bank but not federal bonds; may not impose taxes that 'deprive them of the power to serve the government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes Marshall's reasoning and later Supreme Court clarifications analyzing effect of tax (whether it hinders efficient exercise of federal power). Examples: exemption of federal agencies depends on effect of tax; tax on operations vs tax on property distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: State police and taxation powers limited where they seriously interfere with interstate commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: While states may exercise police power and taxation for local public safety and welfare, they may not seriously interfere with interstate commerce. States can enact local safety regulations even if they incidentally affect interstate commerce (examples: inspection of illuminating oils; quarantine laws; restrictions on Sunday freight trains; requirements for guarding bridges), but laws that effectively prevent interstate shipments or regulate commerce wholesale can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: Kentucky oil inspection sustained; Minnesota meat-inspection law invalidated because it prevented transportation of meat slaughtered elsewhere; Illinois railway rate regulation invalid when applied to interstate shipments; cases over intoxicating liquors and the 1890 congressional act creating uniform regulation discussed. Cites specific cases (Minnesota v. Barber, Patterson v. Kentucky, Railroad Company v. Peniston).

rubrics_metrics.name: States have practically no power over the monetary system
rubrics_metrics.description: States may charter and regulate state banks but cannot coin money, emit bills of credit, or make anything but federal coin legal tender. State bank note issuance is effectively prohibited by federal taxation (1866 act imposing 10% tax on such notes), upheld by the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Veazie Bank v. Fenno and other cases; explains Congress's power over money effectively precludes state monetary independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: States cannot pass bills of attainder or ex post facto laws (criminal legislation limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original Constitution limits states from passing bills of attainder (legislative punishments without judicial trial) and ex post facto laws (laws punishing acts not punishable when committed, adding punishment retroactively, or changing rules of evidence to the accused's serious disadvantage). These limitations apply only to criminal legislation and were intended to prevent retrospective punitive laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (Cummings v. Missouri; Calder v. Bull) and explains the Framers' rationale (prevent British-style abuses).

rubrics_metrics.name: States cannot pass laws impairing the obligation of contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution prohibits states from passing laws that impair the obligation of contracts. 'Contract' is used broadly to include legally binding agreements about property, grants, charters, franchises between private parties or between a commonwealth and private parties. The clause protects franchises, charters, and privileges secured by private corporations from retrospective state legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sturges v. Crowninshield (bankruptcy law invalidated), Dartmouth College case (charter as contract), Bank of Ohio v. Knoop (charter tax rate promise treated as contract). The Court has limited the clause: appointments to public office for fixed term, certain municipal grants, bounty laws, and state liquor licenses have not been treated as contracts; the clause is applied mainly when the law is retrospective and affects pre-existing contracts; provisions allowing future revision avoid invalidation.
